newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives recover in polls, but too slow.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives recover in polls, but too slow.

text.p: Down, but not yet out?
Britain's Conservative party received a boost on Thursday when polling group MORI said the party's support among voters had at last risen significantly -- to 34 percent.

The poll showed Labour's lead over John Major's Conservatives cut to 15 points from 27 in the last poll, and provided evidence the Conservatives are at last taking a lead on Labour on key questions of economic management and taxation.
But, voting experts say, the Conservatives recovery in the polls looks like a case of too little to late.

"The latest polls show an improvement for the Conservatives and suggest they have had a good week (in the election campaign) but they still have a huge mountain to climb to reach the 43 percent of the polls they probably need to form the next government," said Simon Atkinson, political analyst at MORI.

"No one ever expected the huge opinion poll leads Labour enjoyed earlier in the campaign to last right up to election day and a narrower lead of 15 percent for Labour is still a huge advantage for them just weeks ahead of polling day," he added.

Others agree. "This poll result would have to be confirmed by others before it was clear Conservative party support really had taken a step forward and this was not just a rogue poll," said Paul Whiteley, lecturer at the University of Sheffield.

Significantly, a second poll by rival polling group Gallup also published on Thursday showed Labour actually extending its lead to 23 points, only five points less than when the election campaign begun last month.

"The gap between the two parties will certainly narrow between now and election day -- forecasters have always said that. Many polls currently point to a Labour overall majority of some 200 seats, but it is much more likely to be around half that," said Whiteley.
Indeed, even the more slender 15 point lead in the MORI survey would still give Labour an overall majority of around 160 seats, voting analysts said.

A Reuters survey of 20 top voting behaviour experts published on Wednesday showed on average they expect a Labour overall majority of 83 seats in the election in the 659-seat House of Commons, up from a 77 seat average prediction they gave a week ago.
And nineteen of the 20 members of the Reuters panel believe Labour will win the election -- one expected a hung parliament -- and six forecast a Labour majority of more than 100 seats.

But, just three weeks until the election, Conservative strategists will hope the Gallup poll is right and support will keep flowing towards their party, proving the doubters wrong and keeping Labour out of power again. Conservatives are hoping for an action-replay of the 1992 election, when Labour's support crumbled on voting day as many "secret" Conservatives turned up to support their party.

But there are crucial differences between the 1997 and 1992 elections. Ahead of the 1992 election many polls put Labour ahead, but often only by a margin of one or three points, and some even had the Conservatives ahead.
In 1997, by contrast, Labour has enjoyed the strongest pre-election poll lead since world war two, which if translated into votes on election day would result in an historic landslide.

The gap, which many experts now estimate is around 18 to 20 points between the two major parties, will be extremely difficult to close, at least on the basis of the swings parties have achieved during election campaigns ahead of past elections.
Big movements in poll ratings have occured in past elections. In all but two of the past 10 British elections the party leading at the start of the campaign has lost support during it.
But work by political analyst Peter Kellner suggests the huge gap may be unbridgeable between now and May 1. Writing recently in London's Evening Standard newspaper, he notes:

"Even if the Conservatives were to match their biggest ever campaign gain (six points in 1992) and Labour were to match its biggest loss (five points in 1964, 1970 and 1983) Labour would still enjoy a 10-point lead over the Conservatives on May 1: enough to give Tony Blair a Majority of around 100."
Kellner says the electorate will have to prove much more votatile than in previous elections for an upset to occur.
"The most significant swings have often taken place during the final 10 days. Once again, the Conservatives must be hoping that this election breaks new ground," Kellner argues.
